entities.name: Book of Enoch
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Book of Enoch, an ancient Jewish apocalyptic text traditionally attributed to Enoch, the great-grandfather of Noah, is thought to have been composed between the 3rd century BCE and the 1st century CE. This work is significant for its profound influence on both Jewish and Christian eschatology, particularly in its depictions of angels, the afterlife, and divine judgment. It is considered canonical by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, while being excluded from the canonical texts of Judaism and most Christian denominations, showcasing its complex role in religious history.

The text contains five major sections, including the Book of Watchers, which details the fall of the Watchers, angels who descended to Earth and corrupted humankind, and the Book of Parables, which presents a vision of the coming Messiah. Through vivid imagery and prophetic revelations, it addresses the themes of righteousness, divine retribution, and the ultimate triumph of good over evil. The Book of Enoch was influential in shaping early Christian thought, particularly regarding Christ's role as the judge and the nature of the heavenly realm, although its exact date of authorship remains debated.

Despite its exclusion from the Jewish and Protestant canons, the Book of Enoch's legacy persisted through the centuries, influencing various theological discussions and literary works. It was lost to the Western world for many centuries until rediscovered in the 18th century, leading to renewed interest in apocalyptic literature. Scholars and theologians have recognized its impact on later religious texts, including the New Testament, and its role in the development of mystical Jewish traditions such as Kabbalah.

entities.name: Book of Enoch (1 Enoch)
entities.label: Text
entities.summary: A composite Jewish apocalyptic text attributed to the antediluvian patriarch Enoch (Gen. 5:18–24), composed in stages between the 3rd century BCE and 1st century CE. The complete text survives only in Ge'ez (Ethiopic) translation — part of the Ethiopian biblical canon — though fragments were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls in Aramaic. The book comprises five sections: the Book of the Watchers (fallen angels who mate with human women, producing the giant Nephilim — expanding Gen. 6:1–4); the Parables of Enoch (introducing the "Son of Man" figure, a pre-existent heavenly judge); the Astronomical Book (a 364-day solar calendar); the Book of Dreams (apocalyptic visions); and the Epistle of Enoch (ethical exhortation and apocalyptic judgment). 1 Enoch profoundly influenced early Christianity — its "Son of Man" concept is central to the Gospels, and it is directly quoted in the Epistle of Jude (Jude 14–15). Its survival exclusively in Ethiopia makes the Ge'ez literary tradition uniquely important for Jewish and Christian textual studies.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Book of Enoch influenced early Christianity with its apocalyptic visions and the concept of the 'Son of Man', which later appeared in the New Testament as a title for Jesus Christ. Its 364-day solar calendar also had significant regional impact on Ethiopian Orthodox Church.
